rationale: A wins because it finds the sharper editorial tension and does not just turn the release into a market-trend costume party. Its best line, "Databricks claims $3B ARR and 60% growth — unaudited, on its own benchmarks, before any public filing," gives a reporter a real accountability frame. B is strong, but "giving the model away to sell everything around it" gets ahead of the facts and needs a business-model proof point the update did not provide.
gaps_in_A: "Banks and hospitals want AI models they can audit" smuggles in auditability; the update says regulated enterprises, fine-tuning, and closed-API alternatives, not audit rights or audit logs.
"regulated enterprises cannot send proprietary data to third-party inference APIs" is too categorical. Some can, some cannot, and the update does not prove a legal bar.

"the platform — the fine-tuning infrastructure, the data layer, the enterprise support — is where the money is" is plausible Databricks strategy, but it is still inference. It needs exec proof before it becomes the pitch spine.
gaps_in_B: "legally or contractually can't route sensitive data through a closed hosted API" overstates what the update proves. Regulated friction is supplied; legal impossibility is not.
"frontier-quality models" is not grounded. The update says benchmarks are company-owned, so quality claims should stay in the proof bucket.
"Is open-source the new enterprise-AI land grab?" is a trend headline wearing a loud jacket. One Databricks release is not a land grab without comparable vendors or market data.

"giving the model away to sell everything around it" asserts monetization logic before the facts support it, then quietly admits "what the company actually sells around the model" is missing. That is the exact hole a reporter will poke.
